arXiv · mathematics · January 2026 – 13 November 2026

In the wake of AI papers

Count new works on

In November 2026, through the 13th, 54 new arXiv mathematics papers follow up an AI-generated paper: 1.4% of the month’s papers, against 121 in October and 29 in September.

A paper follows up an AI-generated paper when its main result uses that paper’s results, extends them, adapts its method, or re-proves, explains or checks it. Papers that only cite one are not counted. See what counts.

What counts

A follow-up paper is a new arXiv preprint whose main result builds on a document whose authors declare both its proofs and its writing generated by an AI model.

AI-generated works. A document counts as AI-generated when its authors, or its publisher, declare that an AI model generated both its proofs and its text. The list holds 938 works:

  • OpenAI’s October 6 release (github.com/openai/math, 2026), which says its manuscripts were “produced by an internal OpenAI model”: 724 manuscripts in 373 result families (722 in the first release, two added on 26 October, one of them the refutation of the Exponential Time Hypothesis), each family counted as one work.
  • OpenAI’s other mathematics documents, each saying its proofs were produced by an OpenAI model: the disproof of Erdős’s unit distance conjecture (May 2026), the proof of the cycle double cover conjecture (July), “Ten advances in mathematics and theoretical computer science” (August; each of its ten results counted as one work), the improved upper bound for short gaps between primes (August), the improved lower bound for long gaps between primes, the finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes and for the Euler equations (September), and the construction of quantum Yang–Mills theory whose Lean code OpenAI submitted in October to the Yang–Mills Shepherding Committee, which calls it an LLM-produced result.
  • 279 arXiv papers of January to October 2026, in the categories below, whose statement on AI use says a model generated the text and also says a model produced the proofs or the main results. Papers whose statement covers only the writing, credits the model with a named part only (a key idea, an example), or leaves the extent of its part vague are not on the list. Papers of November 2026 join the list once the month closes.
  • 257 works on Hexagon, deposited from September 2026 to 16 November 2026, whose depositor declares the text primarily AI-generated and whose provenance statement says a model produced the proofs, by the same reading as for arXiv papers.
  • Twelve documents added by hand: the manuscript constructing a complex structure on S6 that Claude produced under the direction of L. Alpöge; the proof of the Erdős–Sós conjecture (Erdős problem 548) found by GPT-6 Astra, with the write-up generated from it; the argument improving the lower bound for gaps between primes (Erdős problem 4) posted on erdosproblems.com in August 2026, whose PDF names GPT 5.6 Sol as its author (the site credits GPT 5.6 Pro); and Anthropic’s refutation of the Exponential Time Hypothesis, “A 2o(n) Time Algorithm for 3-SAT” (October 2026), whose byline is Claude and whose core algorithm, it says, an internal Claude model found with no human input; and six results that Wikipedia lists among mathematical discoveries made with AI and whose own account says the model found them: four by GPT-6 Astra in Epoch AI’s evaluations (the disproofs of the Köthe and Ibragimov–Iosifescu conjectures, the proof of the Dittert conjecture, a counterexample to the γ–θ conjecture on eternal domination), Claude’s proof that θ(pc) = 0 for bond percolation on ℤd, and the Kozma–Nitzan connection inequalities produced by ChatGPT 5.6 Sol and Claude Fable 5.1 (September 2026); and the counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture in dimension 3 that L. Alpöge posted on X in July 2026, crediting the Claude model Fable “for working” on it; and the smooth counterexamples to the Loewner and Carathéodory conjectures that he posted in August 2026 after looking at the problem “with a model”, checked, he says, by himself, J.-P. Smith and Claude.

Follow-up papers. A paper follows up an AI-generated work when its main result, as its abstract and introduction present it, takes that work’s result as an input or a hypothesis; extends, improves or makes it explicit; adapts its method; or gives a new proof, an exposition, a formalization or a check of it. Papers that cite an AI-generated work for background, for comparison, to state priority, or in a remark are not counted; the table above gives their number. A paper sharing an author with the work it follows up is counted like any other.

The papers searched. Every new preprint from January 2026 to 13 November 2026 whose primary category is one of 28 arXiv mathematics categories: all of them except General Mathematics, History and Overview, Information Theory and Statistics Theory, with Mathematical Physics. Each paper is read from the source of its first version, and its title, abstract, comments and every source file are searched for the arXiv number, the Hexagon number, the title or the address of a work on the list. Each paper found was then read in full where it cites the work, and classified by Claude; every follow-up reading was checked against the paper’s text. Months are months of submission to August 2026, and of the arXiv number from September 2026.

Disclaimers

The counts record what papers say they do with an AI-generated work, and say nothing about whether any of the mathematics is right.

Not a judgement of correctness. A paper is listed for what it says it does with an AI-generated work: using it, extending it, explaining it, or checking it. Being listed says nothing about whether that paper or the AI-generated work is correct, and some follow-up papers were written precisely to check, or to correct, the work they follow.

Declarations are taken as stated. Whether a document is AI-generated is taken from what its authors or publisher declare; nothing has been verified. A document whose authors say nothing about AI is not on the list, however it was produced.

The counts are lower bounds. Only papers in the categories above are searched, only first versions are read, and a paper that refers to an AI-generated work without naming its arXiv number, title or address (“a recent AI proof of …”) is not found. November 2026 is incomplete, and its own AI-generated arXiv papers are not yet on the list.

Readings can be wrong. Each classification is a judgement made by reading the paper. Corrections are welcome; get in touch.

A study directed by Kimball Martin using Claude. Corpus: every new preprint in 28 arXiv mathematics categories from January 2026 to 13 November 2026, read from the arXiv source of its first version. A companion page follows AI use in arXiv mathematics papers. Papers counts every new preprint of the month in the 28 categories. The share is of that count, with a 95% interval. By an author of the work counts follow-up papers that share an author with every AI-generated work they follow up; they are included in the counts. The table starts in January 2026, the month of the earliest AI-generated paper on the list: no earlier paper can follow one up.

The most followed-up AI-generated works

Each AI-generated work with the number of papers that follow it up. Open a work to see those papers and what each one does with it. Each result family of OpenAI’s October 6 release counts as one work, and so does each of the ten results of OpenAI’s earlier “Ten advances”; ★ marks the release’s headline results. One paper studies the release as a whole and is listed under it.

What counts

A follow-up paper is a new arXiv preprint whose main result builds on a document whose authors declare both its proofs and its writing generated by an AI model.

AI-generated works. A document counts as AI-generated when its authors, or its publisher, declare that an AI model generated both its proofs and its text. The list holds 938 works:

  • OpenAI’s October 6 release (github.com/openai/math, 2026), which says its manuscripts were “produced by an internal OpenAI model”: 724 manuscripts in 373 result families (722 in the first release, two added on 26 October, one of them the refutation of the Exponential Time Hypothesis), each family counted as one work.
  • OpenAI’s other mathematics documents, each saying its proofs were produced by an OpenAI model: the disproof of Erdős’s unit distance conjecture (May 2026), the proof of the cycle double cover conjecture (July), “Ten advances in mathematics and theoretical computer science” (August; each of its ten results counted as one work), the improved upper bound for short gaps between primes (August), the improved lower bound for long gaps between primes, the finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes and for the Euler equations (September), and the construction of quantum Yang–Mills theory whose Lean code OpenAI submitted in October to the Yang–Mills Shepherding Committee, which calls it an LLM-produced result.
  • 279 arXiv papers of January to October 2026, in the categories below, whose statement on AI use says a model generated the text and also says a model produced the proofs or the main results. Papers whose statement covers only the writing, credits the model with a named part only (a key idea, an example), or leaves the extent of its part vague are not on the list. Papers of November 2026 join the list once the month closes.
  • 257 works on Hexagon, deposited from September 2026 to 16 November 2026, whose depositor declares the text primarily AI-generated and whose provenance statement says a model produced the proofs, by the same reading as for arXiv papers.
  • Twelve documents added by hand: the manuscript constructing a complex structure on S6 that Claude produced under the direction of L. Alpöge; the proof of the Erdős–Sós conjecture (Erdős problem 548) found by GPT-6 Astra, with the write-up generated from it; the argument improving the lower bound for gaps between primes (Erdős problem 4) posted on erdosproblems.com in August 2026, whose PDF names GPT 5.6 Sol as its author (the site credits GPT 5.6 Pro); and Anthropic’s refutation of the Exponential Time Hypothesis, “A 2o(n) Time Algorithm for 3-SAT” (October 2026), whose byline is Claude and whose core algorithm, it says, an internal Claude model found with no human input; and six results that Wikipedia lists among mathematical discoveries made with AI and whose own account says the model found them: four by GPT-6 Astra in Epoch AI’s evaluations (the disproofs of the Köthe and Ibragimov–Iosifescu conjectures, the proof of the Dittert conjecture, a counterexample to the γ–θ conjecture on eternal domination), Claude’s proof that θ(pc) = 0 for bond percolation on ℤd, and the Kozma–Nitzan connection inequalities produced by ChatGPT 5.6 Sol and Claude Fable 5.1 (September 2026); and the counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture in dimension 3 that L. Alpöge posted on X in July 2026, crediting the Claude model Fable “for working” on it; and the smooth counterexamples to the Loewner and Carathéodory conjectures that he posted in August 2026 after looking at the problem “with a model”, checked, he says, by himself, J.-P. Smith and Claude.

Follow-up papers. A paper follows up an AI-generated work when its main result, as its abstract and introduction present it, takes that work’s result as an input or a hypothesis; extends, improves or makes it explicit; adapts its method; or gives a new proof, an exposition, a formalization or a check of it. Papers that cite an AI-generated work for background, for comparison, to state priority, or in a remark are not counted; the table above gives their number. A paper sharing an author with the work it follows up is counted like any other.

The papers searched. Every new preprint from January 2026 to 13 November 2026 whose primary category is one of 28 arXiv mathematics categories: all of them except General Mathematics, History and Overview, Information Theory and Statistics Theory, with Mathematical Physics. Each paper is read from the source of its first version, and its title, abstract, comments and every source file are searched for the arXiv number, the Hexagon number, the title or the address of a work on the list. Each paper found was then read in full where it cites the work, and classified by Claude; every follow-up reading was checked against the paper’s text. Months are months of submission to August 2026, and of the arXiv number from September 2026.

Disclaimers

The counts record what papers say they do with an AI-generated work, and say nothing about whether any of the mathematics is right.

Not a judgement of correctness. A paper is listed for what it says it does with an AI-generated work: using it, extending it, explaining it, or checking it. Being listed says nothing about whether that paper or the AI-generated work is correct, and some follow-up papers were written precisely to check, or to correct, the work they follow.

Declarations are taken as stated. Whether a document is AI-generated is taken from what its authors or publisher declare; nothing has been verified. A document whose authors say nothing about AI is not on the list, however it was produced.

The counts are lower bounds. Only papers in the categories above are searched, only first versions are read, and a paper that refers to an AI-generated work without naming its arXiv number, title or address (“a recent AI proof of …”) is not found. November 2026 is incomplete, and its own AI-generated arXiv papers are not yet on the list.

Readings can be wrong. Each classification is a judgement made by reading the paper. Corrections are welcome; get in touch.

A study directed by Kimball Martin using Claude. Corpus: every new preprint in 28 arXiv mathematics categories from January 2026 to 13 November 2026, read from the arXiv source of its first version. A companion page follows AI use in arXiv mathematics papers. Corrections, references and discussion of each manuscript of OpenAI’s October 6 release are collected by an independent community effort, oai-math-revised. Page generated 17 November 2026.
